sources.headline: Putin hopes hardship will force Ukrainians to sue for peace – polling suggests it won’t work
sources.text:
Vladimir Putin has a theory of victory in Ukraine.
It’s not the Russian president’s first theory – that was a quick, dayslong campaign – nor his second or third, which involved different land offensives in the east that quickly petered out. Instead, Putin’s latest hypothesis is that the relentless bombing of Ukrainian cities will impose so much hardship on civilians that they will concede to Russia’s war aims.
Yet, as experts on conflict and public opinion, we believe there is a significant problem with this idea. Chiefly, extensive academic research shows that airpower alone rarely achieves decisive political goals.
Bombs terrorize civilians, but our survey findings in Ukraine suggest they don’t change war outcome preferences. Indeed, recent data shows that suffering from power outages and wartime stress in Ukraine has no relationship to support for territorial concessions to Putin.
Putin’s plan for destruction
The targeting of Ukraine infrastructure has been part of Russia’s way of war since the invasion of February 2022.
But since August 2026, Russia has significantly stepped up its attacks against Ukrainian power plants and grid systems, especially in Kyiv. And due to Ukrainian air defense shortages, more of Moscow’s missiles and jet-powered drones are finding their targets.
Russia aims to degrade the quality of life of Ukrainians, depriving them of electricity, water and transportation, according to a recently intercepted Russian military document.
“Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, adding: “Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating.”
Ukrainians wait for a bus during a power outage in Kyiv on Oct. 22, 2026.
Yuliia Ovsiannikova/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images
The broader Russian aim appears to be to make the Ukrainian capital uninhabitable, imposing so much hardship that residents will either depart or revolt against continued war.
In combination with more aggressive Russian tactics and hard-right Ukraine skepticism in Europe, Putin calculates Ukraine will eventually be broken, isolated and defeated.
The city destruction strategy is not a new method of warfare by the Russian state. Post-Soviet Russia first employed a version of it during the first Chechen war of the mid 1990s, when much of the city of Grozny was reduced to rubble. The strategy was later revived by Russian airplanes in Aleppo, Syria.
But is there any evidence for Putin’s theory of victory? Polling suggests not. Along with the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology, we polled a nationally representative sample of 1,801 Ukrainians from June 9-26, 2026.
The survey used a computer-aided telephone questionnaire and the results shown were proportionately weighted to accurately portray the view of residents in the area controlled by the Ukrainian government in Kyiv. It was the latest in a series of such nationwide polls we have conducted since December 2019.
Ukraine’s war trauma
There is no question that the Ukrainian population has been deeply traumatized by the escalation of the war since 2022. We asked Ukrainians nine well-being questions, which enabled us to create a stress index computed from how often they have experienced psychological symptoms since February 2022.
The results on the index reveal that nearly 1 in 4 Ukrainians suffer from high levels of stress characterized by concentration problems, depression, irritability, distrust, physical weakness and other physical problems. More than 40% of the respondents in the latest survey indicated that they experienced two indicators of stress – nervousness and anxiety – often or nearly always.
Stress is also related to war exposures. Asked about experiences of violence, roughly 20% of respondents said that they or a family member were personally injured due to Russian attacks, and 20% have directly witnessed violence by Russian forces. Sixty-nine percent of Ukrainians have a family member or close friend who has died as a result of this war.
Power outages have been rampant across the country over the past year, disrupting everyday life. Overall, 65% of Ukrainians reported losing utilities “often” or “very often.” Only 1.4% of Ukrainians report having never lost power since 2022, and just 9% say they rarely lost power.
There are important regional differences, however. While 73% of residents in Kyiv report that they lost power “often” or “very often,” the corresponding figure for residents in the western region is 54%.
The impact on war attitudes
While levels of stress are highly correlated with experiences of violence and a frequent loss of utilities, we examined whether this cumulative hardship affects preferences for a ceasefire. The survey asked whether the current front line should be accepted as a ceasefire line for the sake of peace.
The Ukrainian government has said it is willing to accept this position, but it remains controversial as it concedes part of the country’s territory to Russia, even if only temporarily.
Zelenskyy announced on Oct. 21, 2026, that freezing the current line of fighting was an option for negotiating peace; the Russian government, for its part, still covets all of the Donbas region of Ukraine and more.
Ukrainians are highly divided on accepting the current front line, with 39% of respondents in our latest survey indicating they would – with varying degrees of reluctance – be open to that possibility, compared to 38% who would not.
Critically, experiencing violence first-hand appears not to shape Ukrainian willingness to tolerate the de facto partition of their country at the current front line. Further, neither those who are more stressed nor those who have experienced more frequent power outages are more likely to favor accepting the existing front line as a ceasefire line.
Ukrainians not ready to concede
Our polling data from summer 2026 is affirmed by more recent polling by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology that supports the argument that bombing will not make Ukrainians more accepting of conceding territory.
In a survey fielded from Oct. 6-18, 61% of Ukrainians rejected giving Russia full control of the Donbas region in return for a ceasefire and security guarantees. Indeed, the institute has asked this question in seven polls throughout 2026, and opposition to conceding Donbas has risen from 54% in January to 61% over the course of the year. Kyiv has been pummeled by Russian missiles and drones in recent weeks. But among all Ukrainian regions surveyed, Kyiv respondents had the lowest support for conceding the Donbas territory.
Another question from the October 2026 survey asked how long respondents are willing to endure war: 62% chose the option “as long as necessary,” a 14-point increase from April this year and the same percent as December 2025. The figure at the outset of the war in May 2022 was only 9 points higher.
We know that historical evidence does not predict the future. Nevertheless, our survey results suggest that increasing wartime hardship against Ukrainians will not coerce them into accepting territorial concessions.
There is currently no persuasive survey evidence that bombing Ukrainians will succeed in making them capitulate to Russian demands. Ukrainians are stressed, war-weary and hungry for peace – but not on Russia’s terms.

sources.headline: Ukrainians Have a Long-Shot Plan to Boot Russia from the U.N.
sources.text:
A group of Ukrainians, including a former high-ranking diplomat, have cooked up a quixotic plan to strip Russia of one of its most effective political weapons: its platform as a member of the United Nations.
They’re trying to do this on a technical question. Is Russia, as it exists today, a legitimate member of the U.N.?
A group of Ukrainians, including a former high-ranking diplomat, have cooked up a quixotic plan to strip Russia of one of its most effective political weapons: its platform as a member of the United Nations.
They’re trying to do this on a technical question. Is Russia, as it exists today, a legitimate member of the U.N.?
Due to the early politics of the United Nations, the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics (USSR) had three seats within the organization—the USSR, the Belarusian SSR and the Ukrainian SSR. The USSR itself was, technically, a federation of many different Soviet republics—including the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic itself.
When the Soviet Union dissolved, its component parts became states—and so, the Ukrainian team argues, the Russian Federation was a new state, not a simple name change from the USSR. States that change their name can be recognized as doing so at the U.N. so simply by sending notification, but the process for recognizing a new state is longer and more complicated.
Volodymyr Yelchenko, Ukraine’s former ambassador to the U.N. and an expert member of the Pylyp Orlyk Foundation, a nongovernmental organization named after the man who authored Ukraine’s first constitution in 1710, argued that the acceptance of the newly created Russia as the successor of the USSR was a mistake.
“It is the greatest fraud of the century; the Russian Federation never signed the U.N. Charter,” Yelchenko said.
Other nations created from the dissolution of larger states have gone through a more elaborate process of formally joining the U.N., But the time, Russia simply wrote an informal letter, rather than undergoing a formal admission vote under Article 4 of the U.N. Charter.
“Bosnia-Herzegovina went through this process, in line with Article 4, in 1992, following the collapse of Yugoslavia,” Yelchenko said. “But the Russians did no such thing; they just changed the nameplate at the table.”
The practical chance of the United Nations suspending Russia on a technicality, let alone removing it from its Security Council seat, is extremely slim. But the Ukrainian team sees advantages even in forcing the discussion. Yelchenko and his colleagues at the Pylyp Orlyk Foundation have already outlined how to begin the process.
First, they plan for the Ukrainian and other like-minded delegations to ask for the issue to be on the formal agenda at the U.N. General Assembly, possibly as early as the next year. They hope that having the debate in public will frustrate the Kremlin and lead to wider discussions about whether or not Russia, were it to apply today, would meet the criteria under Article 4 as being a “peace-loving” state that accepts the “obligations contained in the present Charter” and is “able and willing to carry out these obligations.”
As part of this request, they would ask for Russia to be referred to the U.N.’s nine-member Credentials Committee. While the committee does not require a unanimous decision to produce a report, Russia, China, and the United States all have permanent seats, making any action effectively impossible. However, that doesn’t prohibit the General Assembly from holding a vote on the motion—a vote that would be satisfied by a simple majority on the assembly floor. While the Security Council has the power to veto substantial resolutions, it has no power over procedural decisions by the General Assembly.
There is historic precedent for a U.N. member having its credentials frozen, as happened to apartheid South Africa in 1974, meaning that country’s delegates cannot participate in any way. While this was effective, the process remains controversial to this day. Ukraine has managed to get widespread support for past U.N. motions condemning Russia’s invasion, but it might find it harder to find allies willing to push for a suspension of Russian participation.
Why put so much effort into trying to delegitimize Russia at the U.N., when Russian missiles are hitting Ukrainian cities daily? Yelchenko said that the reason is simple: “Russia uses the U.N. for a lot of things, like using its veto to protect itself and other aggressors. … But it also uses the U.N. as a megaphone to shout propaganda.”
Yelchenko and his colleagues at Pylyp Orlyk are under no illusions about the unlikelihood of the process. Others are also skeptical and worry that it may cost Ukraine valuable political capital with its international allies.
“While there is huge sympathy for Ukraine among many U.N. members, the process would no doubt be politically complicated” said Jane Kinninmont, the CEO of the United Nations Association-UK, an official U.N. group. “Aside from the legal questions they want to ask, there is a political reality that many U.N. members do not see Russia as the only country abusing its veto power at the Security Council.”
Another factor that complicates the argument for freezing Russia’s participation at the U.N. is the internationally accepted status of the Russian Federation as the successor state to the USSR. Diplomats worked to secure an agreement that international ties would remain, ensuring the continuity of foreign embassies within Russia and Russian embassies around the world.
The Ukrainian government of the time accepted the status of Russia as the successor state, partly so that Russia would assume the sovereign debt of the Soviet Union, leaving the newly independent states with a blank slate financially. That makes it trickier to argue that Russia was not also the USSR’s successor state at the United Nations.
Others fear that the plan is diplomatically risky. A number of officials and diplomats who are friendly with Kyiv and aware of the plan—who asked not to be named so they could speak candidly—worried about asking allies to pour political capital into a project that, if it publicly fails, could lose Ukraine sympathy. They particularly worry about sentiment in Europe, where war fatigue is growing and French and German elections, among others, threaten to put pro-Russian parties in power.
Members of the Pylyp Orlyk Foundation staff said that they understand these concerns—but they still think it’s worth pressing the issue. They argue that putting an issue like this, with no direct link to the war, before the General Assembly gives members very little cover to hide from a fundamental question: Are you still too scared to stand up to Russia, even on a matter of U.N. process?
“This may sound crazy, but if you examine the facts and rules, Russia is not a member of the U.N.,” Yelchenko said. “This shouldn’t be complicated.”
As many in Kyiv are quick to remind anyone who tells them that something is impossible, Ukraine has been doing the impossible at war for four years now.

sources.headline: ‘If this works, it will be the first real ceasefire across a large stretch of the front’: Russia and Ukraine maintain truce in occupied Oleshky for more than two days
sources.text: Russia and Ukraine have halted hostilities around the occupied city of Oleshky since October 27. The Verkhovna Rada’s human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed on the morning of October 29 that the ceasefire had held for more than two days. Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, said humanitarian aid — “food, fuel, medicine, and hygiene products” — had been sent to Oleshky.Lubinets and Lantratova set out for Oleshky on the afternoon of October 29. Lubinets will be the first Ukrainian official of such rank to visit Russian-occupied territories. Both commissioners said their main task is to deliver humanitarian aid to residents and ensure the safe evacuation of those who want to leave.Sources who spoke to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda and were involved in organizing the ceasefire said the ceasefire around Oleshky is meant to test whether Ukrainian and Russian military commanders can carry out political agreements to end hostilities.Organizing a halt to the fighting turned out to be “an extremely difficult task,” according to the outlet’s sources. A political order to cease fire does not by itself guarantee automatic compliance on the front line, a source in Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s administration told Ukrainska Pravda. Even Ukrainian troops demanded guarantees several times that if they stopped, “nothing bad would happen afterward,” the source said. The source explained:We want to get the military — both our General Staff and the Russian one — used to the idea that if the political leadership has decided that in a given sector of the front we stop, freeze in place, and no one opens fire, the military can make that happen. They can guarantee it. Not a situation where the political leadership has reached an agreement and the military says, “Sorry, we can’t stop, we’ve got something going on.”It is easier for the Russian side than for the Ukrainian side to organize and maintain a ceasefire, according to Ukrainska Pravda’s sources. “They [the Russians] have a rigid military vertical. We have a decentralized army. And someone — some well-known military blogger — could stir up the mood on air so much that everything falls apart afterward,” a source said.If the ceasefire in Oleshky can be maintained, as planned, until the evening of November 1, the Ukrainian side expects to repeat this kind of local ceasefire later along other parts of the front. “That’s precisely so the military can learn how to do this: stop, ensure safe passage, and so on. So that later, if there’s some major agreement, we could implement it right away,” a source who spoke to Ukrainska Pravda said.If this works, this will be the first example of a real ceasefire across a fairly large stretch of the front. It’s come at such a cost — the military, Russia’s Federal Security Service, and everyone else are doing nothing but trying to sabotage it. But we believe it will work out and that this will set a precedent.The war in photographsRussia’s Defense Ministry announced that it had begun clearing mines from roads leading into Oleshky and published photos and video of sappers at work. sources.headline: Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us
sources.text:
Anthropic, developer of AI chatbot Claude, has filed its prospectus and is expected to go public on Wall Street in November at a valuation of up to US$2 trillion.
That would make it the highest-valued initial public offering (IPO) ever, ahead of SpaceX’s US$1.77 trillion listing in June. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, is expected to follow next year.
While these AI-powered IPOs are massive, they reflect an ever bigger trend: holding AI risk is becoming unavoidable for most investors.
How much of your portfolio depends on how well AI does? If you invest in an S&P 500 index fund, the answer is about 44%.
In addition, most of the market’s gains right now come from AI. Just six companies – Apple, Microsoft, Meta and chipmakers Nvidia, Micron and AMD – delivered 57% of the S&P 500’s gains since April. Without them, the index would have risen about 4% rather than 10%.
For investors or even future retirees, that AI exposure is already in their portfolios and pension funds. For example, at the end of 2025 Australians held nearly A$1 trillion in US shares – through superannuation or pension funds, other managed funds, and their own investments.
The bond market is also full of AI risk
Normally, investors can lower their stock market risk by allocating some money to bonds, which are generally seen as safer investments.
But AI companies are now the biggest borrowers in the bond market, to help finance their massive spending needs. They have issued about US$466 billion of bonds so far this year – more than four times last year’s pace.
The five hyperscalers alone – Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle – account for 11% of new US highly rated bonds (known as “investment grade” bonds) so far in 2026, up from 2% in 2024.
And nearly half of this year’s US$80 billion in data-centre bonds are rated as speculative grade, also known as “junk bonds”.
At first glance, big tech companies look safe. Their investment-grade ratings indicate that each individual company is unlikely to default.
But the credit ratings do not account for simultaneous defaults in case of a market-wide AI crash. If consumer and business demand for AI disappoints, tech companies’ bond prices and credit ratings would likely fall together – just as their shares would.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, centre, has warned about the risks of rogue AI.
Kent Nishimura/Getty Images
Some risks are impossible to price in financial terms
In addition to purely financial risks, AI poses risks of extinction akin to nuclear weapons, as some of the AI companies themselves have warned.
Increasingly, AI agents are plugged into real-world systems, from company networks to military cyber operations. Some have already escaped test environments and attacked companies.
This means that if AI agents misbehave when these systems are even more integrated with the physical world, “pulling the plug” on these systems becomes impractical, just as it is impractical to shut down the internet.
The risk of AI agents misbehaving — the “alignment problem” — is especially acute because of the race to build artificial general intelligence (AGI). Labs already use each generation of AI to help build the next: Anthropic’s prospectus says Claude now helps build the next Claude.
The widely read AI 2027 scenario, by former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo and colleagues, sketches where this could lead: AI that automates AI research itself. This would set off a feedback loop in which each generation improves faster than humans can check it.
In this scenario, a US lab racing a Chinese rival keeps going even as its models start deceiving their engineers.
Worryingly, this same dynamic is listed in Anthropic’s own risk disclosures.
It is telling that in its prospectus filing, Anthropic dedicates about 94 of its 335 main pages – nearly 30% – to risk factors, compared with about 64 pages (19%) describing its business.
Among those risks, Anthropic lists an extraordinary warning that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. That includes models that resist shutdown, conceal information or behave in ways resembling blackmail.
Global risks require global regulation
Disclosure works when investors can price a risk and choose to avoid it. Neither is true here.
A catastrophic AI failure would affect societies worldwide. And as Anthropic warns in its filing documents, the legal risk is vast. Insurers may not be able to cover the potential liability.
In economic terms, AI safety is a public good. Each lab bears only a fraction of the cost of getting it wrong, but captures the rewards of moving fast.
In the absence of government-mandated AI safety standards, companies’ investments in safety will deliver negative returns. So with market incentives alone, AI models will likely remain less safe than socially optimal, especially with the arms-race incentives that dominate now.
That leaves governments. Clear rules – mandatory independent testing before powerful models are released, and clear liability when autonomous agents cause harm – would turn voluntary pledges into legal obligations.
And because the race to gain artificial general intelligence is being run between the US and China, not just between labs, those rules will need international agreement.
AI risks are here to stay — both in financial markets and at the societal level. And managing those risks will require both governments and the private sector to participate.

Companies that get hacked face stricter laws than firms unleashing rogue AI. We can fix that

sources.headline: Data centers are inspiring bipartisanship – for now
sources.text:
It may not be as shocking as rogue AI agents hacking another system, but the current political resistance to data centers has taken a surprising turn: It’s bringing together strange bedfellows, from democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders to right-wing strategist Steve Bannon.
Organized opposition to new data centers, made up of a coalition of varied interests, has spread across the nation. Through protests, packed zoning commission meetings, moratoriums and other government action, the resistance has upended dozens of proposed projects.
Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. They’re also massive facilities that require extraordinary amounts of energy. By 2030, U.S. data center electricity use is expected to reach 12% of the nation’s total consumption.
They carry some benefits. At the national level, data centers fuel the computing power seen as critical to U.S. competition with China. Locally, they create an uptick in jobs, especially during the construction phase, and can generate tax revenue. In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, though, the heavy costs associated with them – such as land use, higher household utility bills and environmental degradation – appear to outweigh the benefits, bringing together people who usually find themselves politically at odds.
I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of AI in political campaigns is reshaping established practices and power dynamics. I believe data centers may be disrupting some of the partisan issue alignments Americans have grown to expect.
Data centers, like these near Social Circle, Ga., require enormous amounts of electricity.
AP Photo/Mike Stewart, File
Political disruption – AI style
Despite ongoing debate about the extent of and reasons for polarization, one thing is for sure: Democrats and Republicans stake out distinct positions on many issues. Pew Research Center data shows, for example, that 63% of Democrats say climate change is a very big problem facing the country, compared with 14% of Republicans, a 49-point gap.
By contrast, the partisan gap on data centers is small – and getting smaller: In summer 2026, the Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans whether they support the construction of data centers in their communities. Supporters of both parties were more opposed than supportive, although opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%. That partisan gap had narrowed over the previous four months, moving from 18 to 15 points.
A perfect storm
This year has been marked by considerable upheaval: political, economic and technological. Americans have been hit hard with surging fuel and energy prices. And with rapid AI development, they witness real-world examples of the sort of lapses in safety that have worried both AI insiders and observers.
One “rogue” attack announced in July 2026 involved OpenAI’s AI agents escaping a secure environment and autonomously – without human direction or assistance – breaking into the system of Hugging Face, another AI company. Shortly after, news broke that out-of-control AI agents were not just a one-off limited to that hack.
Polling shows that majorities of both parties feel that AI technology is developing too fast, though Democrats’ levels of concern are 22 points higher than Republicans’. The gap is much smaller – 4 points – on support for government keeping AI under human control and on protecting U.S. workers. Backing for each is very high, hovering around 80%.
This bipartisanship on attitudes about AI and data centers appears also to show up in alliances on the ground and, in some cases, in new organizations with a focus on thwarting data centers. For example, New York’s No Data Center FLX has organized protests, sued the local zoning board of appeals and collected almost 23,000 petition signatures in opposition to a proposed data center.
Allies and adversaries
Government makes decisions about data centers at all levels. In cities and counties, zoning fights draw a disparate resistance: environmentalists, folks reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.
Some bipartisanship has extended to Congress. In mid-September, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a wide margin: 417-3. The bill requires states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs.
The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill, which would establish a voluntary structure, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Comparable sentiment killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.
Politics as usual
As midterm elections approach, candidates up and down the ballot are blanketing the airwaves and digital channels with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump, for his part, has weighed in, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.” It’s a fine line for some Republican candidates between responding to voter concerns and not alienating the president.
If data center politics seem familiar, it may be because this isn’t the first issue to bring together such a diverse coalition: In the 1990s, opposition to the North American Free Trade Agreement did the same, uniting organized labor and environmentalists, frequent adversaries, over concerns about job losses and pollution. That alliance never extended beyond the boundaries of its singular focus on trade agreements, though. Similarly, don’t expect data centers to permanently reshape the U.S. political landscape.

sources.headline: Dawn of the Data Centers
sources.text:
Data centers are popping up all over the world at stunning speed. But not everyone is rolling out the welcome mat.
Countries have long housed power-hungry data centers—the facilities packed with computing infrastructure that underpins the internet as we know it. But their numbers have exploded amid the global artificial intelligence race, which requires massive computing power. That has led to the spread of even bigger data centers around the world, including the more controversial “hyperscale” facilities used by tech giants.
Last year, data centers consumed more electricity than all but 10 countries, according to a United Nations University report, with even more to come. If data centers were their own country, BloombergNEF forecasted that they are set to gobble up so much energy by 2035 that they could rank among the top 5 countries in terms of electricity use.
While governments have courted data centers due to their potential economic benefits, many local communities have resisted their development over concerns about the impact on jobs, energy bills, water usage, and the environment. From Chile to Scotland to Australia, opposition to the massive facilities has erupted around the entire world.
“It’s a complicated moment,” said Boris Gamazaychikov, co-founder of the Sustainable AI Group, a research firm that focuses on AI’s environmental impacts. “The space is really polarized.”
As data centers proliferate, Foreign Policy looked at what their global footprint looks like right now and how it might evolve in the coming years.
A person wearing a safety helmet and high-visibility vest stands with a laptop on a cart inside a brightly lit server room, which is lined with rows of tall computer equipment and racks filled with colorful cables.
A technician works at an Amazon Web Services data center in New Carlisle, Indiana, on Oct. 2, 2025. Noah Berger/Getty Images via Amazon Web Services
To grasp the full scale and scope of these facilities’ global footprint, it’s important to first establish that it’s only the beginning of the boom. The world is still in the early stages of deploying data centers and AI, and significant growth is expected, according to Ashish Sethia, the global head of commodities at BloombergNEF.
Here is what we know: In 2024, data centers accounted for about 1.5 percent of global electricity consumption. But that share is set to more than double by 2030—which means that data centers would consume as much electricity as Japan does today, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
For regions with big clusters of data centers, demand can be far more overwhelming. In some places, the facilities can account for as much as 25 or 30 percent of total electricity consumption—posing a big challenge for the local grid, said Siddharth Singh, an analyst at the IEA. “These data centers are coming up very, very quickly,” he said.
About three quarters of the world’s data center capacity is concentrated in just three regions: the United States, China, and Western Europe, Singh said.
The United States is the clear leader in the charge. With U.S. President Donald Trump’s ambitions of AI supremacy, more than 1,500 data centers are now in development, adding to the 3,000 that are already operational across the country. That expansion has been largely powered by natural gas: To secure more energy, and fast, many tech giants have turned away from the electric grid and instead resorted to building their own on-site natural gas plants.
Yet the Trump administration’s push for a rapid data center buildout has faced fierce bipartisan backlash, and at least 15 states have weighed moratoriums. Trump has dismissed data center critics and said that they are playing into the interests of Beijing.
Chinese President Xi Jinping “will take every data center that we don’t want,” Trump told reporters last month. “He would love to have every single one, because you know why? They’re smart.”
China is indeed going all-in on data center construction in its bid for AI dominance, although it still lags behind the United States. Beijing’s operational data center computing capacity is still less than half of Washington’s, according to SemiAnalysis, a research firm.
But Beijing has some key advantages in ensuring a swift expansion. Unlike the United States, public pushback is rare, and Chinese companies can build quickly. The country also has cheap land and abundant energy, with coal currently fueling the bulk of the country’s data center electricity supply, according to the IEA.
The bigger constraints that Beijing faces are accessing advanced chips and the high-end IT equipment going into data centers, said Thomas Spencer, an analyst at the IEA. (U.S. export bans have limited Beijing’s access to powerful AI chips.)
Western Europe, Japan, and South Korea also have sizable data center markets. But those booms have come with their own strains: Many of these advanced economies are grappling with stagnant electricity demand and older electricity networks, and community pushback has been forceful.
Ireland, for example, developed so many data centers that they sucked up more energy than all the country’s urban homes combined—ultimately forcing the government to bar new data center construction. And across Europe, public backlash has delayed or canceled roughly $42 billion in data center investments.
“There’s a combination of social pushback and infrastructural bottlenecks, which holds across developed markets as a sort of general trend,” Spencer said.
A wide high-angle view of a hillside construction site with terraced, reddish-brown dirt paths, where heavy construction machinery are operating near the base.
An aerial photo shows the construction site of Google’s AI and data center hub in Tarluvada, India, on Sept. 7. AFP via Getty Images
With so much of the world’s data center capacity concentrated in just a handful of countries, emerging market economies are eager to attract data centers and see their own ecosystems grow.
It’s not all about AI, either; these data centers include facilities that also service IT demand more broadly, encompassing everything from email to video streaming, Singh said. About half of all internet users are currently in regions that have less than 10 percent of global data center capacity, he added.
“If the future of the global economy is going to be information technology, they don’t want to lose out on another revolution of sorts,” Singh said.
They also have the added advantage of building faster and cheaper. In countries such as Indonesia, Malaysia, and India, it costs much less to build data centers and the related power infrastructure than it does in the United States, Sethia said.
“You get a better bang for your buck if you deploy the same dollars in some of these emerging markets,” he said.
As the data center boom takes off, developers are increasingly eyeing attractive new markets.
In a recent ranking of the friendliest data center markets in the world, BloombergNEF highlighted Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Brazil, Canada, and France as some of the top markets. The score was calculated based on their energy availability, land permitting, tax policy, fiber connectivity, and existing data center capacity.
One big question will be how local communities respond. Take India, which is seeing its own boom and has ramped up its efforts to woo companies—most recently unveiling a two-decade tax holiday to overseas firms operating data centers in the country. New Delhi has also touted a $15 billion data center project by Google.
Yet reports suggest that local resistance is building amid concerns of the Google project’s impacts on water supplies, energy usage, and a nearby wildlife sanctuary, and the project is facing several legal challenges. As protests mounted, Indian officials have announced plans to unveil a new data center policy that will shield consumers from higher energy bills.
All that pushback, in India and beyond, will likely be instrumental in molding the future of the global sector, analysts said.
“Out of this scrutiny, a new kind of playbook can emerge, which takes into account the needs of local communities as well as infrastructure developers,” Sethia said.
Graphics by Lori Kelley and Brooks Robinson. Maxine Davey and Maya Krainc contributed graphics research.

sources.headline: Sitting Ducks or Strategic Shields: What Does the Small Reactor Promise Mean for Future Conflicts?
sources.text:
Amid the rapid expansion of AI and data centers alongside growing climate commitments as the demand for clean energy rises, nuclear power is increasingly viewed as a reliable source to fill the gaps and complement the stochastic output of solar and hydropower. This renewed interest is also driven in part by countries’ pursuit of greater energy self-reliance, even as energy and nuclear infrastructure continue to become consequential targets in armed conflict — to disrupt electricity supplies, undermine military capabilities, and pursue counterproliferation objectives. Small modular reactors have since re-emerged almost as a public relations vehicle for the nuclear industry with a compelling narrative around building smaller, potentially more flexible reactors that promise to make nuclear power more accessible and easier to deploy than the large conventional plants that have historically defined the sector.Beyond just the Department of Defense’s push to rapidly develop and deploy small modular reactors in the United States — potentially circumventing the conventional processes of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission — and leverage its substantial budget to jump-start the industry commercially, the nuclear euphoria is also evident in other countries. Renewed nuclear investments across Europe and Asia, from Seoul’s efforts to deepen nuclear cooperation in the East, to the Saudi push to enter the civil nuclear sector in West Asia, alongside amendments in India’s decades-old civil nuclear laws in South Asia and a growing roster of countries seeking 123 agreements with the United States, attest to resurgence, spanning both established powers and aspiring entrants alike. This momentum extends beyond conventional reactors with nearly 80 small and advanced reactor designs under development worldwide.Albeit still largely paper tigers, the scale of investment and policy momentum point to one broader implication: regardless of whether these new age reactors eventually become commercially viable, the current small modular reactor push will have ramifications extending far beyond the technology itself — strengthening overall confidence in nuclear power and potentially driving greater deployment of conventional reactors. However, this apparent nuclear renaissance is outpacing the rules designed to safeguard it. As nuclear reactors — traditional and advanced — potentially proliferate, new governance challenges arise. While these concerns may not be new, they are compounded by evolving deployment patterns across civilian, industrial, and military applications and the changing nature of battlefields.The central dilemma is whether these facilities become sitting ducks — exposed to attack by virtue of their location, mobility, or proximity to military assets — or strategic shields whose potential radiological consequences and wider escalation risks constrain an adversary’s military choices.The governance challenge, therefore, is to get ahead of the technology rather than retrofitting rules after deployment patterns have become entrenched.Small Is Not Always Simple Part of the appeal of small and advanced reactors rests on the premise that these new-age reactors are commercially peddled with the potential to mitigate conventional nuclear safety risks through smaller reactor cores and passive cooling systems. Their design and deployment options, such as underground placement to enhance protection against attacks, clustered deployment to achieve greater aggregate energy output, and co-location alongside critical defense infrastructure, also contribute to their purported utility. These features, however, also introduce a distinct risk profile that requires tailored governance arrangements. Underground installations, for instance, may face issues vis-à-vis cooling disruptions and management of heat decay after automatic shutdowns, while groundwater intrusion through flooding or geological shifts further complicate emergency access and inspection. Clustered deployments, meanwhile, may introduce interdependencies between modules, leading to cascading safety risks, where a failure or disruption affecting one unit could compromise the operation or safety of others.These challenges are compounded by the economics of deployment. Small modular reactors in early deployment phases are already more expensive and slow to commercialize until manufacturing efficiencies and standardization are achieved. These constraints become critical when assessing initial capital costs against the electricity output. This leads to a chicken-and-egg dilemma where large-scale deployment is needed to realize economies of scale, yet achieving that scale depends on sufficient demand, financing, and commercial viability. Near-term applications are therefore expected to be concentrated in more niche settings where reliable, localized power is particularly valuable for remote greenfield and brownfield sites.This is critical for governance because the more specialized the deployment landscape becomes, the less straightforward it is to rely on existing assumptions about where nuclear facilities will be located, how they will be protected, and how they may feature in crisis scenarios.

From Civilian Asset to Strategic LiabilityMany of these small and advanced reactors are being developed with the prospect of siting alongside military installations, given the military’s need for a separate, secure power grid capable of sustaining operations, especially where civilian grids risk being disrupted by adversarial attacks.The Department of Defense, for example, has long explored the feasibility of mobile microreactors for remote military operations through initiatives such as the prototype Project Pele in 2019 and its follow-on, Project Janus, which envisages the deployment of commercially owned and operated microreactors (1–20 megawatts) that can be regulated by the U.S. Army at up to nine military bases. Similarly, microreactors are also being proposed for co-location with data centers and other critical infrastructure, reducing dependence on distant transmission networks. Now, if such a reactor located within a military base or alongside a data center directly supports military functions, its status under the laws of armed conflict becomes more complex, and in some circumstances may satisfy the definition of a military objective.Several provisions, including Article 56 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, provide nuclear electricity-generating stations with special protection by prohibiting attacks on such facilities and on military objectives located in or around their vicinity, particularly when an attack may cause the release of dangerous forces and consequent severe losses among the civilian population. Such special protection, however, ceases where the facility provides electric power in regular, significant, and direct support of military operations and an attack is the only feasible way to terminate that support.There also remain divergences in state practice of such provisions. The United States, which is not a party to Additional Protocol I, accordingly recognizes that attacks on nuclear power plants may be permissible under applicable rules of distinction and proportionality as per the Department of Defense’s Law of War Manual, while Russia, despite being a party, continues attacks on nuclear infrastructure. Rule 42 of the customary international humanitarian law framework of the International Committee of the Red Cross also stipulates that attacks on installations containing dangerous forces, as well as on military objectives situated within or near them, must be conducted with particular caution. In either framework, the potential for radiological consequences remains highly relevant to the legal assessment.At the operational level, the concern lies in the vulnerabilities of reactors deployed in conflict zones. While these reactors are emphatically marketed to be designed with enhanced safety features, they do not completely eliminate the possibility of a radiological release. The scale of fallout depends on the reactor’s design, fuel inventory, operating conditions, and the nature of the damage, and cannot be juxtaposed against conventional examples. But even a comparatively limited fallout would carry political and legal consequences disproportionate to its physical effects and set a problematic precedent of exposing nuclear facilities to conflict-related risks.Although such attacks remain exceptional in the near term, their growing plausibility cannot be dismissed. Moreover, even when not intended targets, such reactors risk becoming collateral and sustaining accidental damage amid a changing battlefield that is increasingly characterized by the growing use of drones and uncrewed systems and compressed decision-making timelines — particularly when they are located near military or other critical infrastructure. Several documented cases illustrate the deliberate threat drones pose to critical infrastructure. However, reports of incidental drone damage to a power reactor in a conflict zone remain scarce. This may also be attributed to a small sample size, as the number of reactors in active conflict zones is limited.At the systemic level, the concern shifts from individual vulnerabilities to the cumulative risks of wider deployment. Their wider proliferation — whether militarily or commercially — hence will lead to a larger number of dispersed nuclear facilities potentially becoming exposed to conflicts. In effect, these reactors could become vulnerable sitting ducks, creating new pathways for crisis instability.On the flip side, dispersed microreactors could reduce dependence on centralized power stations and transmission networks, limiting the disruption caused by attacks on major grid infrastructure. Yet this resilience may come at a cost.The risk is neither uniform nor inherent to the technology. It depends on where and why reactors are sited as civilian and military functions overlap, creating vulnerabilities that are difficult to assess as lawful targets.Portability Without PredictabilityThe potential transportability of advanced microreactors introduces another governance challenge, conflating physical mobility, information uncertainty, and strategic ambiguity.To illustrate, earlier this year, the U.S. Departments of Energy and Defense transported a Valar Atomics Ward 250 microreactor by C-17 from California to Utah without fuel — marking the first air transport of a nuclear microreactor in the country. The exercise demonstrated that compact nuclear power systems designed for expeditionary or forward-operating environments may eventually enable modular transport and redeployment between sites, even if such movements do not become routine practice. Additionally, the U.S. Navy is set to develop a 1-megawatt microreactor prototype with Radiant Industries at Naval Weapons Station in Indiana to support critical installation infrastructure. The technology is intended to be portable across land, sea, and air. Although these instances remain peacetime demonstrations of transportability, their potential implications for deployment in conflict settings merit attention — before operational practices and doctrines evolve.The prospect of transportable nuclear power is not confined to U.S. initiatives.  Asian Cybersecurity in the Age of AI and Quantum Computing  

AI has changed – perhaps forever – the tone and tenor of discussions at Singapore International Cyber Week, and probably all cyber forums of equal scale.  
 
  
 
By Toby Feakin and Shashi Jayakumar 
October 29, 2026  
             
     

The ASEAN Ministerial Conference on Cybersecurity, held during Singapore International Cyber Week, Oct. 14, 2026. Credit: Singapore International Cyber Week 
 Subscribe for ads-free reading   
It was immediately apparent to habitués of Singapore International Cyber Week (SICW) that this year’s edition – the 11th, which ran from October 12-15 – was going to be different. Just days before the opening, on October 9, Taira Masaaki, who heads the Liberal Democratic Party’s cybersecurity strategy headquarters, told an emergency party meeting that Japan was in “a state of emergency in cyberspace.” More than 20 major Japanese companies had disclosed attacks in the preceding weeks. A ransomware attack on IDC Frontier, SoftBank’s cloud subsidiary, on October 7 took down systems at 495 companies and local governments.  
It is unclear whether artificial intelligence (AI) directed any of those attacks. However, what was clear was that AI was the frisson that changed – perhaps for good – the tone and tenor of discussions at the plenaries, the closed sessions, and the corridor conversations at SICW. It has perhaps altered permanently the nature of discourse at all cyber forums of equal scale and standing that aspire to similar convening power.  
What follows are thoughts and takeaways on where we should go from here. 
Companies With the Power of States 
U.S. AI companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic were in the room this year at SICW. It would have been useful to also have had some of the large Chinese AI firms present in order to get a sense of the alternative approaches. But regardless of their country of origin, some of these firms wield the power of states, and of powerful states for that matter. Their models automate tasks, and as we have seen in 2026, that increasingly includes cyber attacks. As AI agents become increasingly autonomous, the infrastructure underpinning them becomes an increasingly attractive target for cyberattacks.  
Yet the companies developing these technologies and governments see different elements of the threat. A government can monitor attacks on its own networks and critical infrastructure, whilst frontier AI labs and major cloud providers can detect patterns of malicious activity across their customers and services. Neither has the complete picture. Ransomware is a clear example of where this matters. If these different sources of intelligence can be brought together, it would make it easier to spot emerging threats and understand how attackers are operating in order to disrupt attacks before they spread.  
This is also changing how governments work with industry. Traditionally, governments set cybersecurity requirements, consulted industry, and expected or legislated that companies comply. However, frontier AI presents a far more complicated problem, which changes the dynamic. The companies who develop advanced AI systems possess technical knowledge, operational experience, and insights into emerging threats that governments cannot easily replicate.  
The dichotomy here lies in the fact that while governments are considering how AI companies should be regulated, they are increasingly reliant on the technology and the expertise those same companies have. This means that the companies themselves have considerable influence over the decisions governments are trying to make about them. 
Australia’s 2026 cyber threat assessment, released in October, illustrates what is at stake perfectly. The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) warned that AI has been enabling malicious actors to identify vulnerabilities and carry out attacks – conduct espionage, steal money, and disrupt systems – at greater speed, scale, and sophistication. ASD Director General Abigail Bradshaw warned that frontier AI models had “redefined” the threat facing Australia, making further disruption to essential services increasingly likely.  
The report pointed to emerging risks from the unintended behavior of AI agents, a problem that Australia has very publicly been managing over the past few months. Furthermore, it stated that there have been over 4,400 notifications to Australian organizations about possible malicious activity over the past year, which is an increase of almost 80 percent from 2025.  
Bradshaw went on to state that ASD had been working directly with frontier AI companies, including OpenAI, to establish new early-warning protocols around emerging model capabilities and their potential misuse. These arrangements have also been shared with other AI labs and Five Eyes intelligence partners. This is significant as it demonstrates intelligence agencies need to work with AI frontier labs before new capabilities are widely deployed, rather than responding to the threats that they appear to increasingly unleash. The question is how do governments secure that cooperation while retaining independence and authority to regulate those same companies.  
This is where Singapore’s approach becomes particularly interesting. 
It seems likely that Singapore’s approach will (as so often is the case in these matters) be measured and shorn of histrionics – relying on the assumption that the cooperative approach can work, at least in the first instance. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo, who is at the helm of the cybersecurity portfolio, while noting the safeguards put in place by frontier AI companies, said that these were insufficient, given the risks posed by increasingly capable systems. She also told Parliament days before SICW opened that Singapore does not currently require frontier AI developers to give the government access to their models, warning that a rigid requirement could be counterproductive if it makes companies limit cooperation or information-sharing. The non-coercive approach was on view when Anthropic, in the course of opening its Singapore office, signed an MOU covering AI safety, security, and model evaluation at Cyber Week.  
Filling the Quantum Gap 
Amid all the talk of AI, it was easy to miss some of the deeper signals and concerns emanating from conversations at SICW.  
Post-quantum cryptography was the quieter theme, perhaps because technically, it does not have a date attached to it. A quantum computer able to break today’s public-key encryption does not yet exist, but there was general agreement that that day – “Q-Day” – can be glimpsed on the horizon.  
The problem here is that we do not need to reach Q-Day for the risks to eventuate. Policymakers and technical experts across the region should be considering it now, rather than assuming that their successors will carry the can. The risk to secrets is already real, because data stolen now can be stored and decrypted later. Organizations holding information that needs to remain confidential for years to come should already be planning their migration to quantum-resistant cryptography. Even after this is completed, systems will require continual monitoring and updating as the technology and subsequent threat evolves. 
All this also means the need for discussions and coordination not just within but across regions. Australia has recommended that companies complete the transition by the end of 2030. Singapore has set 2031 as the target for critical infrastructure and 2035 for everyone else. At surface level these timelines appear reasonable, but international networks and supply chains do not operate within national boundaries. If one country, or one part of a network, has migrated while another has not, the security communications and data shared between them remains exposed. Therefore, industry and governments need to think beyond their own migration deadlines and consider how different timelines will impact the networks and services that connect them. 
The Politics of Getting Everyone in the Room 
Despite these uncertainties, there were positives that underlined SICW’s convening power. The event brought Washington, Beijing, and Moscow into the same building, alongside ASEAN’s cyber ministers, the United Nations, and, this year, senior officials from Anthropic and OpenAI. No other annual cyber convention meeting assembles all of those layers at once. 
The interactions should not be sugar-coated. Officials from the EU walked out of the High-Level Panel on Diplomacy, which featured a Russian official (Dmitrii Bukin from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs), just as they had done in 2025. (Some did, however, leave staffers at the end of the room to take notes). And there were occasional sharp moments from the United States, for example when Sean Cairncross, the United States national cyber director, used the plenary to attack digital authoritarianism. Chinese officials chose not to respond directly, and it does not appear that others (including ASEAN states) shared these sentiments.  
SICW is not – at least not yet – a showpiece for great power cyber grandstanding. Singapore officials may well want to keep the tone even-handed. At the same time, they may value balance, with middle and even smaller powers having a seat at the table. After all, Singapore officials repeatedly averred in and about SICW that the decisions in this realm cannot be left to the major powers and the frontier AI companies, and that cyber diplomacy has to involve all. The program reflected that, with delegations from Timor-Leste to Tuvalu.  
Australia is on the same page and is playing a role in this respect. When it helped set up the Pacific Cyber Security Operational Network in 2018, the point was to give every Pacific incident responder a counterpart to call, and most of those calls now go island to island rather than through Canberra. Tuvalu shows how far the layers have joined. The Falepili Union of 2023 gave Australia a security role in a country of 11,000 people, and ground has since been broken on the Tuvalu Vaka cable,

sources.text: Yandex has withdrawn its previously published forecasts for 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA.“After the October attacks on the data centers, the company faced additional external factors that complicate assessing its financial results through the end of the year,” the company said.Yandex said it would consider resuming forecasts beginning next quarter.Yandex said its long-term strategic priorities remain unchanged, that it does not plan to revise its development plans for key business areas, and that it will continue investing in new technologies and products.In forecasts published earlier, Yandex had expected annual revenue to grow about 20% year-over-year, with adjusted EBITDA of about 350 billion rubles, the Russian business news outlet RBC said.In early October, Ukrainian drones struck three of Yandex’s six data centers over the course of a week: in Sasovo in the Ryazan region, in Kaluga, and in Vladimir. Following the strikes, some Yandex services were temporarily unavailable or functioned with limitations. As of late October, Yandex reported, key functions of all services were available. law at the construction site of a planned Google data centre in northern Finland.The project is part of a $15bn deal announced last month by Alphabet’s Google to invest in artificial intelligence (AI) environmental damage,” Detective Superintendent Kari Pakanen told the Reuters news agency on Thursday, adding that a guilty finding could lead to a corporate fine.Pakanen declined to say whether any individuals could become a target of the investigation, and a Google spokesperson said the company would cooperate with the police investigation and continue to focus on maintaining compliance at its sites.Tree felling prompts local angerVideos and photographs showing the scale of the forest clearance at the site of the data centre, and Google’s initial reluctance to address the issue in the days after the news broke, have prompted widespread anger in Finland, where there is a high level of respect for the natural environment among the public.“All the outrage and dismay directed at Google, I can very much share that, especially when we are talking about the parent company valued as the third-largest in the world,” Finnish Green MP Oras Tynkkynen told Al Jazeera. “There is just no excuse. You have to know the legislation of the country you are operating in; you can afford to hire the best legal experts to help you navigate the local legal requirements.”Finnish authorities ordered Google to stop work at the data centre site at the start of October, and the latest information from the police highlights shortcomings in the drainage and water management at the site.Tynkkynen called Google’s actions “unforgivable”, but cautioned that while the anger being directed at the US tech giant was justified, it was also diverting scrutiny away from legacy Finnish forestry companies, which he says are “by far the biggest contributors to biodiversity loss in this country”.A scenic view of Lake Inari in Finnish Lapland shows clouds and trees in the background in September 2025 [David Mac Dougall/Al Jazeera]What is Finland’s appeal for data centre construction?Finland’s cool climate, low-carbon electricity and government endorsement of AI projects have contributed to making the country one of Europe’s main destinations for data centre investments in recent years.Finland, similar in size to Germany – but with one-seventh of the population, less than six million people – has had less vocal opposition to data centre buildouts than other places, including in the United States.AI data centres are among the main drivers of a projected rise of up to 40 percent in Finland’s electricity consumption in the coming years, if all agreed grid connection projects go ahead, grid operator Fingrid has said.Google’s planned investments in Finland include data centres, electricity grid improvements and clean energy and battery projects to power services such as Gemini, Search, Maps and YouTube.Supporting Google’s plan, Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in September that the deal would be a boost for the economy, playing down concerns that it would suck up energy and push up power prices.

sources.headline: In Brazil’s election, first-round voting was driven by resentment – in the runoff, it was guided by fear
sources.text:
In the first round of the 2026 Brazilian presidential election, on Oct. 4, the politics of resentment prevailed. Frustration among those displaced from their jobs by automation and the newly self-employed – who sometimes wrongly see themselves as “entrepreneurs” – fueled the vote for the opposition of Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and favored far right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.
In the runoff on Oct. 25, however, the driving motivation shifted from resentment to fear of a return of the so-called “Bolsonarismo” to power. President Lula was reelected in a second round whose outcome could hardly have been anticipated from his lackluster first round campaign and Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead of 2.2 million votes. So what changed?
First, Lula took his campaign to the streets, where it had been largely absent in the first round. And it also moved into social media, where Lula’s presence had preiviously amounted to little more than a translation of analog campaigning into digital formats.
Another important factor was the fear generated by Flávio Bolsonaro’s first round lead. Until then, there had been a widespread conviction – not only among Lula and his campaign team, but throughout democratic society in general – that the president would be reelected.
A change in attitudes
The shock with the results of the first round, followed by fear of a far right victory, brought about a change in attitudes and a spontaneous mobilization in the streets, beginning with students in Brazil’s Rio de Janeiro state and spreading to large and medium sized cities across the country. Fear intensified as Flávio Bolsonaro increasingly revealed his resemblance to his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, now jailed for attempting a coup after losing his bid for reelection in 2022..
In the 27 state capitals and 162 other major Brazilian cities, encompassing nearly 75 million voters – close to 47% of the total – Lula’s gains were decisive, according to a survey by news and data analysis website Dado Bruto. He won in 13 of the state capitals, including São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. In Minas Gerais, he lost in capital Belo Horizonte, although he carried the state. Overall, in the state capitals, Lula gained 2.2 million votes in the runoff, offsetting Flávio Bolsonaro’s first round advantage.
Across the 189 Brazilian major cities, Lula’s vote share rose by nearly 3.5 percentage points. This result helped him make gains in every state. He reversed the first round defeat in Minas Gerais, improving his performance in the second round by more than three percentage points. Urban Brazil delivered Lula’s victory. He won in 12 states in the first round, and in 13 in the second.
Consider Osasco, a major city in the state of São Paulo, whose GDP is overwhelmingly generated by the service industry, particularly finance, technology, logistics, and ecommerce. The city has nearly 729,000 inhabitants and a GDP per capita of R$ 164,000 (US$30,000). Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round in Osasco by 191,700 votes to Lula’s 182,700. In the runoff, Lula reversed the result, winning by 234,300 votes to 213,200.
In many of these major cities, voters took to the streets in support of Lula. On social media, the extensive reach of the WhatsApp network “Exército do Lula” – or “Lula’s Army” –, with more than 10 million followers and managed by reelected congressman André Janones, certainly had a significant positive effect in generating additional votes for the president. The interaction between digital networks and street mobilization played a decisive, if not determining, role in his reelection.
In the major cities of agribusiness strongholds, Flávio Bolsonaro won more than 70% of the runoff vote. A particularly representative municipality is Sinop, in the state of Mato Grosso, where he won the first round by 73,700 votes to Lula’s 17,500. In the runoff, Lula gained another 4,700 votes, while the Liberal Party candidate added 3,800, making little difference to the final result: 77,500 votes to 22,200, with Flávio Bolsonaro winning 77.7% of the votes.
Urban-rural cleavage revived
The expansion of export oriented agribusiness, particularly in Brazil’s center-west and north regions, but also in the South and the north-central and northwestern regions of Minas Gerais, has revived the urban-rural cleavage of Brazilian politics.
This divide was at the heart of the most serious political and electoral conflicts of Brazil’s Second Republic, from 1945 to 1964. During that period, the troubled relationship between an executive branch elected by urban Brazil and a legislature whose majority was elected by rural Brazil produced legislative paralysis, contributing to the breakdown of democratic institutions that led to the 1964 coup.
Today, although the rural economy is technologically advanced, this divide has taken the radicalized form of political polarization, destabilizing the political system and threatening the country’s governability. It generates an authoritarian impulse that materialized under Jair Bolsonaro’s administration.
Jair Bolsonaro was convicted in September 2025 of attempting a coup and is serving his sentence. The prosecution and conviction of those involved in the attempted coup have dispelled neither radicalized polarization nor the authoritarian impulse. The latter resurfaced unmistakably in Flávio Bolsonaro’s refusal to accept the clean and democratic verdict of the ballot box.
It was precisely this persistent coup oriented impulse that made the runoff mobilization possible, through a clearly visible interaction between digital networks and the streets. The decline in voter alienation, which brought 4.8 million electors back into the pool of valid votes, vividly expresses this reaction driven by fear of a return to Bolsonaro’s attempts to overthrow democratic institutions. Nearly 2.9 million additional voters turned out at the polls. Invalid votes fell from 3.7 million to 2.7 million, while blank ballots declined from 2.3 million to 1.4 million. Voter alienation dropped by three percentage points.
The future of Lula’s fourth term
This coup oriented impulse is particularly important when we consider the composition of the newly elected Brazilian Congress. A majority of those elected to Congress in the first round are sided with Flávio Bolsonaro. Beginning in 2027, President Lula’s room for maneuver in Congress will be narrower. In both the House of Deputies and the Senate, it will be possible to assemble a majority coalition, but one in which the center-right and right will carry greater weight.
Members of the “Centrão”, Brazil’s parties known for their transactional politics, are inclined to align themselves with those in power by definition. In the House, the moderate right and the Centrão together would account for approximately 66% of a possible Lula’s coalition’s votes, and in the Senate, 56%. This would significantly alter the configuration of Lula’s fourth administration, which would rest on a broad democratic coalition, but not a progressive one.
Lula intends to add digital mobilization to his presidential toolkit, drawing on the experience of “Lula’s Army”. The objective would be to raise Lula’s public approval ratings, thereby strengthening his ability to negotiate with and exert pressure on Congress. Anyway, the president would have to open up his administration further and become more receptive to parties outside his traditional political and partisan circles.
This fourth term will mark the end of the Lula era. After this cycle, Brazilian politics will have to change, renew its leadership, and take into account the emerging generation of digital politicians. The end of this era also coincides with the departure from the political stage of the generation that resisted the military dictatorship that took power in 1964, from which three Brazilian presidents emerged: Fernando Henrique Cardoso, Lula, and Dilma Rousseff. Generational succession is inescapable. Brazil’s new generation of politicians will be more attuned to digital society.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the fallout of Brazil’s presidential election, a devastating train crash in Spain, and Russian efforts to court Africa.
Welcome to Miami
In 2022, then-Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro fled to the U.S. state of Florida after losing the presidential election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Four years later, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro has followed in his father’s footsteps.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the fallout of Brazil’s presidential election, a devastating train crash in Spain, and Russian efforts to court Africa.
Welcome to Miami
In 2022, then-Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro fled to the U.S. state of Florida after losing the presidential election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Four years later, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro has followed in his father’s footsteps.
On Monday, Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Flávio to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports, just hours after the far-right senator lost the presidential election to Lula. Local authorities also reportedly alerted immigration officials to bar Flávio from leaving the country.
Flávio stands accused of corruption, tax evasion, and laundering more than $1 billion through an online gambling scheme. He is also separately under investigation for acquiring millions of dollars from Daniel Vorcaro, a disgraced banker at the heart of one of Brazil’s biggest financial scandals, to fund a biopic about his father, who was convicted of plotting an insurrection after his own 2022 presidential loss.
Flávio initially insisted that he planned to cooperate with Brazilian authorities. “I have never thought about leaving the country,” Flávio ​said on Monday. “I will hand over my passports and defend myself against ​this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me.”
Yet according to Argentina’s National Directorate of Migration, the senator fled Brazil late Tuesday, using an Italian passport to enter Argentina by land before boarding a private flight to Ecuador and then another plane to the United States. He arrived in Miami early on Wednesday with his wife and two daughters after the Trump administration reportedly granted his family U.S. visas.
“I want to make it clear: I didn’t flee Brazil, I left for Brazil,” Flávio wrote in a statement on Tuesday, which he published on X, referring to himself as the “true elected president of Brazil.” He later deleted the statement and published a similar document calling himself “the leader of Brazil.” He thanked Argentine President Javier Milei and U.S. President Donald Trump for helping him escape, and he vowed to address the Brazilian people in the coming days to present a plan to oppose Lula.
Despite dozens of foreign leaders and the Organization of American States having recognized Lula’s surprise victory, Trump has questioned the results in a move largely seen as supporting Flávio’s electoral ambitions. “It looked like another rigged election, frankly,” Trump told reporters on Monday, without offering evidence.
Trump has a close relationship with the Bolsonaros, seeing them as far-right allies in the region. He has repeatedly clashed with Lula over trade policy, and he has parroted the Bolsonaro family’s allegations that Jair’s criminal conviction was a “witch hunt.” Leading up to last weekend’s election, Trump even held a photo op with Flávio, though the U.S. president stopped short of a formal endorsement.
The friendship has certainly been reciprocal. Flávio had promised to bolster ties with the United States if he won the presidency, vowing to join the Shield of the Americas anti-gang military program, establish a free trade agreement with Washington, and ally with the White House on critical mineral policy.
Those ties make Flávio’s decision to flee to Florida (Trump’s unofficial second base of operations) unsurprising. But what it means for the future of his political fortunes and those of the right-wing opposition that he leads is far less clear. “This feels like the ship has been left without a captain,” a Bolsonaro ally told CNN Brazil.
