Deadly train crash. Spain suffered another train-related trauma on Wednesday, after the collision of two high-speed trains near the city of Toledo killed at least 68 people and injured around 100 others. Search-and-rescue operations are still underway.
The accident occurred early on Wednesday after an information technology failure involving railroad switching equipment stopped all trains on the heavily trafficked Madrid-Sevilla rail line. A train from Iryo, a competitor to the Spanish national rail line, stopped on the southbound tracks shortly after 8:30 a.m. local time. A few minutes later, the central control of Spanish rail gave the go-ahead for another southbound train from the state carrier RENFE to continue its journey through a roughly 15-mile stretch on the outskirts of Toledo, according to Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente.
The train is believed to have reached a speed of around 120 miles per hour when it slammed into the stalled Iryo train on the same track. “It was an accident that was truly inconceivable,” Puente said in a press conference.
The accident comes at a sensitive time for the Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who is facing a reelection fight in November. In January, a high-speed train derailment on the same line killed 46 people. And earlier this month, another high-speed train between Madrid and Barcelona caught fire, raising questions about the Spanish government’s oversight and maintenance of one of the world’s largest high-speed rail networks.—Keith Johnson
Putin courts Africa. This year’s two-day Russia-Africa summit kicked off in Moscow on Wednesday with a focus on bolstering the Kremlin’s reach on the continent. “The era when the destinies of entire continents were determined by a narrow bloc of states is coming to an irreversible end,” Russian President Vladimir Putin said, alluding to Moscow’s efforts to outbid China, Europe, and the United States for regional influence.
Putin emphasized Russia’s grain and fertilizer deliveries to more than 40 African countries; called for expanding Africa’s decision-making role in the U.S.-dominated World Bank and International Monetary Fund; and doubled down on Moscow’s security presence in the region, specifically with its paramilitary Wagner Group. Expanding ties with Africa could also help the Kremlin circumvent the impact of European sanctions.
Yet African nations may not be as enthused to strengthen ties with Moscow. Only around 22 African leaders attended this week’s summit, a significant drop from past years’ attendance. Some experts suspect that this is due to anger over Russia’s use of African soldiers in its war with Ukraine. “Security means little when young Nigerians are lured abroad and end up on a frontline they never chose,” Nigerian newspaper Vanguard wrote in an op-ed on Tuesday.
Britain’s budget proposal. British Finance Minister John Healey unveiled a highly anticipated 2027 budget plan on Wednesday that aims to help households weather surging energy bills and high fuel prices. The proposal is the first by Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government, which has made economic reform and fiscal discipline among the top items on its agenda.
According to Healey, the plan envisions giving around 20 million lower-valued homes a roughly $133 payment to help offset rising costs, extending a freeze on fuel duty rates until at least July, and abolishing standing gas bill charges for 23 million households. These energy-focused savings measures are in line with Burnham’s other efforts to provide Britons with price stability amid supply chain crises fueled by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Among the budget’s other proposals, Healey vowed to reduce government borrowing from 4.2 percent of GDP this year to 3.4 percent of GDP next year, remove import duties on more than 100 products, increase the national minimum wage, and raise taxes on gambling and banks. This is a “budget for the worker, the sole trader, the parent at the school gate,” Healey said, adding that his proposal hopes to eliminate the current deficit and “get Britain’s finances into the black” within three years.
Critics, however, remain unimpressed with Healey’s promises, arguing that the timeline for relief could be slow and that energy shocks will likely still be felt by many Britons. The proposal also delayed addressing several major concerns, such as how exactly Healey will increase defense spending and continued public anger toward high taxes, until next year.
Odds and Ends
A Belgian chocolate competition is giving Willy Wonka a run for his money. Confectionary artisans from around the world gathered in Antwerp, Belgium, this week for a two-day chocolate sculpture contest. Participants of the World Chocolate Masters showcased several intricate creations, from a bird vase to an elf to an original video game character. But the winner of the event went to Italian chocolatier Tommaso Grollero, whose octopus sculpture earned him the highest overall score.

 Lula’s Election Win in Brazil Is a Relief for China  

Lula’s victory secures the most important destination for Chinese foreign direct investment in the Western Hemisphere and ends a winning streak for Trump-supported candidates.   
 
  
 
By Ricardo Lopes Kotz 
October 29, 2026  
             
     

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a signing ceremony at the Great Hall of the People, Beijing, May 13, 2025. Credit: Ricardo Stuckert / PR

On October 4, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva finished the first round of Brazil’s presidential election behind his main rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro and an open ally of U.S. President Donald Trump. Flavio Bolsonaro had taken 47 percent of valid votes against Lula’s 45 percent. Because no one topped 50 percent of votes, however, the race went to a second-round runoff. 
The first post-election poll gave Bolsonaro a six-point lead in the head-to-head contest. Three weeks later, Lula won with 51.76 percent, a margin of roughly 4.3 million ballots, securing an unprecedented fourth term. His victory came after intense popular demonstrations in leading cities such as Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Belo Horizonte, as well as a new social media strategy boosted by political allies.  
Lula’s comeback matters well beyond Brasília. Since late 2025, Latin America has seen a regional shift toward right-wing regimes. Bolivia, Chile, Honduras, Costa Rica, Colombia, and Peru all elected conservative governments, most of them endorsed by Washington.  
Brazil was meant to be the crowning piece of Trump’s foreign policy, seeing as it is the largest market in the region and one of the only ones who did not agree on Trump’s Shield for the Americas initiative. Instead, Brazil has opted for a pragmatic foreign economic policy, trying to negotiate with both China and the United States.  
The Donroe Doctrine Meets Its Limits 
Washington’s strategy has been referred to as the “Donroe Doctrine,” claiming the United States’ right to assert its interests in the region in security terms. In practice that has meant rewarding ideological allies and treating Chinese influence as a central opposing force.  
A series of electoral victories seemed to confirm the effectiveness of Trump’s approach to the region. Rodrigo Paz ended two decades of Movimiento al Socialismo (MAS) rule in Bolivia in October 2025. José Antonio Kast won Chile in December. Nasry Asfura took office in Honduras after Trump threatened to cut aid if he lost. In June 2026, Colombia elected the Trump-endorsed outsider Abelardo de la Espriella, and Keiko Fujimori finally won Peru on her fourth attempt. Moreover, Argentina’s right-wing President Javier Milei continues to be an ally.  
Tensions between Brazil and the United States have been accumulating in Trump’s second term. In July 2025, the U.S. president imposed tariffs of up to 50 percent on Brazilian goods over the prosecution and later incarceration of Jair Bolsonaro and sanctioned the Supreme Court judge overseeing the case.  
On May 26, 2026, Trump received Flavio in the Oval Office, and on June 2, a day after his administration proposed a fresh 25 percent tariff on Brazilian goods, Trump praised him publicly. Flavio asked Washington to postpone the tariffs until after the voting period, but it was too late: a Datafolha poll found that 52 percent of Brazilians saw the tariffs as an effort to help his campaign, but ultimately hurting the Brazilian economy.  
Until 2030, Brazil and Mexico, the two largest economies in Latin America, will be governed by center-left leaders, both of whom refuse to pick a clear side between Washington and Beijing. For a doctrine premised on sorting the hemisphere into aligned and unaligned camps, this is a strategic setback for Trump, precisely at a moment where the leader faces low approval rates at home.  
Beijing’s Geoeconomic Influence in the Region Is Growing 
For China, Brazil is now a strategic partner. In 2025 it was the single largest destination for Chinese outbound investment worldwide, absorbing 10.9 percent of the total, according to the China-Brazil Business Council (CEBC). Chinese investment in China reached $6.1 billion, up 45 percent, far outpacing both Brazil’s overall foreign direct investment (FDI) growth of 4.8 percent and China’s global outbound growth of 1.3 percent.  
Overall Brazil accounts for almost two thirds of China’s FDI in South America, with a total stock of $85.5 billion, distributed across 355 projects, between 2007-2025. 
China continues to invest heavily in Brazil’s electricity sector, spanning renewable generation and transmission. Automotive investment rose 66 percent to $965 million as BYD began production at the former Ford complex in Camaçari, Bahia (Northeastern Brazil), and Great Wall Motors at the former Mercedes-Benz plant in Iracemápolis, São Paulo. Geely has sealed an alliance with Renault do Brasil and plans local production in Paraná (Southern Brazil) this year.  
Beyond investment, bilateral trade hit a record $171 billion in 2025. China bought nearly 80 percent of Brazil’s soybean exports. These ties survived even Jair Bolsonaro’s hostile rhetoric. But a Flavio government that owed its political capital to Washington would have faced intense pressure to slow Chinese investment, and it would have inherited brand-new legal tools to do so (more on this below).  
After his loss, Flavio Bolsonaro immediately fled Brazil, heading secretly to the United States via Argentina, amid fears of being convicted of ties to money laundering schemes.  
Brazil and the Race for Technology and Critical Minerals 
Lula signed Law 15.506/2026 on September 16, creating Brazil’s first National Policy on Critical and Strategic Minerals (PNMCE) and a council, the CIMCE, attached to the presidency. The stakes for investors are considerable: Brazil holds the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves and leads global niobium production, with newly found lithium and nickel reserves.  
China still controls roughly 90 percent of rare earth processing and magnet manufacturing and the United States was seeking to secure privileged access to exploration of this sector in the Brazilian market.  
The new law has two main aspects: promotion and regulation. The first key is promotion in an industrial policy style. Brazil’s government will provide up to 7 billion Brazilian real in support for firms aiming to raise production and processing of critical minerals, as well as tax credits of up to 1 billion real a year between 2030 and 2034, tied to value-adding and processing on Brazilian soil.  
The second aspect is regulation. The newly formed council, led by the president, must approve direct or indirect changes of control in companies holding rights to critical minerals, as well as international supply agreements that could affect Brazil’s economic or geopolitical security. 
On paper, this created a screening mechanism that can be used as a hurdle for Chinese state capital, depending on the elected administration. A senior official at the Ministry of Mines and Energy said in October that scrutiny would concentrate on business groups or financing backed by foreign governments, while purely domestic deals may be exempt.  
Today, the most visible foreign investors in Brazilian rare earths are American. In April 2026, USA Rare Earth acquired the Serra Verde Mining Complex, Brazil’s only commercial producer of rare earths, for $2.8 billion, in a deal backed by the U.S. government, including $565 million in direct funding from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.  
Meanwhile, between 2024-2025 three Chinese state-owned enterprises invested more than $1.2 billion in acquisitions of copper, nickel, niobium and lithium mines in Brazil. BYD has held lithium rights in Minas Gerais region since 2023. 
Under Lula, the CIMCE is likely to wield screening as an industrial policy filter, asking how much value stays in Brazil. The new law rewards precisely what Chinese firms can offer and Washington struggles to: refining know-how, battery materials capacity, and captive demand from EV plants already operating in Brazil. Under a Flavio government, however, the same powers could easily have been aligned with Washington’s geoeconomic de-risking agenda.  
Beijing’s position in Latin America rests less on ideological affinity than on economic gravity. Even the leaders that are sympathetic to U.S. regional influence, from Kast in Chile to Fujimori in Peru, still count China as their largest trading partner, and the Chinese-built port of Chancay now anchors Peru’s Pacific trade, for example. Brazil, on the other hand, remains a non-aligned political actor and a market where Chinese firms already have an established presence in EVs and energy.  
The new critical minerals law suggests that there will be ample competition in the future, as long as investors can also earn their place by processing locally, even as the dispute for geoeconomic influence in the region continues to grow in different sectors and areas.

sources.text: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Flávio Bolsonaro arrived in Florida on WednesdayByVanessa BuschschlüterLatin America online editorThe defeated candidate in Brazil's presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro, has referred to himself as "leader of Brazil" in a letter he published on social media after leaving the country for the United States. Bolsonaro lost to his left-wing rival, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in the run-off on Sunday by a difference of 4.4 million votes, but has not conceded defeat. In the letter, Bolsonaro alleges, without offering evidence, that he was the victim of "electoral fraud" and says that he will lead the opposition from the US.He left Brazil on Tuesday after failing to comply with an order to surrender his passports, a decision which Lula described as "a shameful act".Figure caption, Watch: Has Flávio Bolsonaro left Brazil to evade justice?Bolsonaro starts his letter, which he posted on his X account, saying "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the leader of Brazil".However, he had posted a previous version, that was later deleted, in which he wrote: "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the rightful president of Brazil."Both versions repeat the allegation that Bolsonaro first made on election night, that an extension of polling hours on Sunday had benefited his rival. In the letter, he says it was "an electoral fraud unfolding before my eyes".The extension was requested by both Lula's and Bolsonaro's campaign teams, and the head of Brazil's electoral authority has said that the vote proceeded normally and in full accordance with the country's laws and constitution.An analysis of election data conducted by BBC Brazil and BBC Verify has also found that only around 34,000 people voted during the extended hours - far lower than the 4.4 million votes that separated Lula from Bolsonaro.In his letter, Bolsonaro also addresses his departure from Brazil - which caused confusion after he disappeared for more than 24 hours.It later emerged that he had gone across the land border to Argentina, and from there flew on to Florida, following a brief refuelling stop in Ecuador. Bolsonaro left after failing to hand in his passports to police - in defiance of a Supreme Court order, which had been issued as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering.He has not been charged as part of the money laundering probe and denies any wrongdoing, calling the investigation a "politically-motivated witch hunt".Bolsonaro added that he had never intended to leave Brazil, but argued that he was the victim of "political persecution".He ended the letter by saying: "I left Brazil but I haven't abandoned Brazilians".While Flávio Bolsonaro said that he planned to lead the opposition from the US, it was not clear how he planned to do that.His party recognised the election result and while some of its politicians have described Bolsonaro as a "political exile", his campaign manager, Rogério Marinho, stated on Wednesday that "there is no evidence" of the electoral fraud that Bolsonaro alleges took place. It is also not yet clear where Bolsonaro intends to stay or for how long. His younger brother, Eduardo, has been in self-imposed exile in the US since March 2025, saying he was the victim of political persecution. The two siblings posted a photo of themselves holding a Brazilian flag on Wednesday. Image source, Eduardo Bolsonaro/Instagram/ReutersImage caption, Flávio Bolsonaro's brother Eduardo posted a photo of the two of them in the USThe Trump administration has provided visas for Flávio Bolsonaro and his family but did not say what kind of visas they were.The US president did not explicitly endorse Bolsonaro in the run-up to the election and told reporters he "won't get involved" when asked about Bolsonaro's allegations of election fraud. Earlier in the week, he had said that "it looked like another rigged election," without providing any evidence.And on Thursday, Trump told reporters that "the election was a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil".

sources.headline: Flavio Bolsonaro lands in US, declares himself 'leader' of Brazil
sources.text:
Brazilian right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro declared himself the rightful leader of Brazil after landing in Miami with his family on Wednesday.
Bolsonaro fled Brazil after the Supreme Court asked him to hand over his passports so he couldn't leave the country.
The right-wing senator had not conceded defeat in Sunday's presidential election to rival, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who often goes simply by Lula.
Bolsonaro lost elections on Sunday and alleged irregularities. His party has acknowledged the results of Sunday's elections and international observers have observed it was fair. The chief of the Brazilian electoral authority said Wednesday that vote proceeded normally and in full accordance with the country's laws and constitution.
The Bolsonaro's were escorted to a vehicle under cover of umbrellas Image: Eva Marie Uzcategui/REUTERS
In an initial open letter posted to X, Bolsonaro declared himself the "elected president." He then deleted the version and updated it with another letter in which he said he was the rightful "leader" of Brazil.
Bolsonaro faces criminal investigations into alleged financial crimes before the country's Supreme Court. But he has cast those investigations as a political witch hunt against his family by left-leaning justices.
"I want to say, not only to my 60 million voters but to the Brazilian people, that I am the leader and that the criminals who stole Brazil’s election are part of a criminal organization that has established a ​tyranny," he said in the updated version.
Asked by reporters at Joint Base Andrews about Bolsonaro's comments, US President Donald Trump declined to comment, reiterating earlier views on how it was "a very strange election."
The US State Department has said it will grant Bolsonaro and his family US visas.
Flavio Bolsonaro flees to the US from BrazilTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
When did Bolsonaro arrive and how did he reach Miami?
Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters were seen disembarking a Gulfstream G400 plane and heading into the Miami-Opa Locka airport on Wednesday morning. Their journey across the Americas had captured regional attention.
The quartet first flew into Argentina late on Tuesday, then took a private jet to the Ecuadorian city of Guayaquil. From there, they continued to Miami, in Florida.
Bolsonaro would lose his immunity from prosecution in February when his term in the Senate ends. On Monday, he had said in an Instagram post that he had no intention of leaving the country and that he would "hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
According to the AFP news agency, Bolsonaro also holds Italian citizenship and so was able to travel despite his Brazilian and diplomatic passports being canceled.
Bolsonaro's flights out of Brazil and towards Miami had been tracked overnightImage: Eva Marie Uzcategui/REUTERS
Potential source of strain between Trump's US and Lula's Brazil
Bolsonaro's departure and his arrival in Florida — like his father Jair Bolsonaro before him after Brazil's previous presidential elections — could deepen a rift between the two most populous countries in the Americas.
During the election campaign, incumbent leftist President Lula had accused the Trump administration of colluding with the Bolsonaro family in a bid to help them return to power.
After the election results, Trump appeared to question the integrity of the vote, saying he thought the extension to voting times was a "very bad look." He had also alleged in the past that Jair Bolsonaro was the victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.
Bolsonaro senior is now in jail in Brazil on charges of leading a conspiracy designed to keep him in power despite defeat in 2022's presidential election.

sources.headline: Trump says won’t ‘take sides’ in Brazil election, but calls it a ‘disgrace’
sources.text: Comments come after Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro fled to Miami in the US and claimed, without evidence, that vote was stolen.United States President Donald Trump declined to say if he agreed with the outcome of Sunday’s presidential elections in Brazil, but said he thought the contest was a “disgrace”.“I thought the election was a great embarrassment to the people of Brazil,” Trump said in response to a question from a reporter on Thursday morning. “I watched the election. I didn’t take sides. I let it be. I was asked not to take sides by the president, the current president,” he said. “But when I watched what went down in Brazil, it was a disgrace…take a look at the market, I mean their market went down through the floor.”Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3President Lula calls Bolsonaro’s Brazil exit ‘shameful’list 2 of 3Flavio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after losing Brazil’s presidential electionlist 3 of 3What’s next for Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro after election defeat?end of listTrump’s remarks came a day after former Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and his family fled Brazil and landed in Miami, Florida, in the US on Wednesday.Bolsonaro and his family were aided in their journey out of Brazil by Trump and his administration, the New York Times reported Thursday. Officials told the newspaper that the US government would likely provide the Bolsonaro family permanent residency.On Sunday, Bolsonaro had lost a run-off election for Brazil’s president to the left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by more than four million votes. The Brazilian real dropped against the dollar by 12 percent in spot trading after the election.Brazil‘s Supreme Court had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports shortly after the election, in an attempt to make sure the right-wing senator did not flee the country before he could be investigated for embezzlement and money laundering.Bolsonaro left Brazil under cover of darkness, crossing by land with his wife and two daughters into Argentina, where the government of Trump’s right-wing ally President Javier Milei had granted them visas. The family then took a small private plane to Ecuador and later on to Miami, where they landed on Wednesday morning.Shortly after landing, Bolsonaro issued a statement saying he was “the true elected president of Brazil” and the allegations against him were “a politically motivated witch-hunt”. He asked the international community “not to normalise what is happening in Brazil” and said he would lead the country’s opposition from the US. He did not provide evidence supporting his claims.Bolsonaro’s own Liberal Party said on Monday that it was accepting the outcome of the election.Although Brazil and the US have had an extradition treaty for several decades, it is unclear if Washington would turn over Bolsonaro, or whether Brazilian authorities would actually indict him and ask for such a move. On Wednesday, Brazil’s Supreme Court dispelled rumours that a search warrant had been issued for his home.Flavio’s father, Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro, undertook a very similar journey to Florida after he lost his bid for re-election in 2022. While he was in the US, the elder Bolsonaro’s supporters attempted to orchestrate a coup. Some in Brazil had called for the country to seek his extradition from the US. He later returned to Brazil and is currently under house arrest there.
